one_liner: Rust BLAKE2b/2s/2bp/2sp crates with AVX2/SSE4.1 kernels; its BLAKE2b hashes about 1.8x faster than OpenSSL SHA-512 in its own benchmark.
what_it_does: Two crates, blake2b_simd and blake2s_simd, implement the full BLAKE2 spec: variable output length, key, salt, personalization and tree parameters, plus the parallel BLAKE2bp/BLAKE2sp variants. The API is Rust-native: one-shot blake2b(input), a Params builder that yields an incremental State (update/finalize, plus std::io::Write), a blake2bp module, and many::hash_many/update_many for hashing a batch of independent inputs at once. The output is a BLAKE2 digest, not SHA-1/SHA-2, and there is no C ABI. A blake2 command-line tool ships separately as the blake2_bin crate.
how_it_is_fast: The SIMD kernels are Rust intrinsic ports of Samuel Neves' blake2-avx2. Single-message BLAKE2b runs a one-lane AVX2 compression with row diagonalization and shift-or rotations; the code comments note these beat the byte-shuffle rotations on recent chips because of an LLVM bug, and LLVM turns them into AVX-512 rotates when that is enabled. The bigger win is multi-lane hashing: BLAKE2bp and many::hash_many transpose the state and message words of 4 independent BLAKE2b jobs (8 for BLAKE2s) across 256-bit AVX2 registers and compress them together, roughly doubling throughput over one-lane BLAKE2b. The best kernel is picked at runtime with is_x86_feature_detected!.
when_to_use: Rust code on x86-64 with AVX2 that needs BLAKE2 specifically, for example Argon2, Zcash/halo2, Substrate or multihash compatibility (crates.io lists 234 reverse dependencies, including sp-crypto-hashing, rust-argon2 and ff).

Hashing many independent messages in batches of at least many::degree() (4 for BLAKE2b and 8 for BLAKE2s on AVX2), such as content-addressed chunks or Merkle leaves, where hash_many roughly doubles per-core throughput over one-at-a-time BLAKE2b.
Replacing SHA-512 or SHA-1 in a design you control, on CPUs without SHA-NI, where the README's 1 MB benchmark shows BLAKE2b at 2.81 cpb against OpenSSL SHA-512 at 5.11 cpb.
Keyed hashing or MAC use, via BLAKE2's built-in key/salt/personal parameters, which avoid HMAC's double hashing (the author's explanation in issue #32).
Embedded or no_std Rust that wants a spec-complete, fuzzed, portable BLAKE2 (CI covers armv7, aarch64, i586 and big-endian powerpc64/s390x).
when_not_to_use: Anywhere SHA-256/SHA-512/SHA-1 output is required (interop, FIPS, certificates, git objects). The digests differ, and BLAKE2bp/BLAKE2sp also differ from plain BLAKE2b/BLAKE2s.

New designs where you are free to pick a hash. BLAKE3, from the same author, ran at 0.95 cpb on the same laptop, about 3x faster than blake2b_simd's BLAKE2b at 2.81, and the author points users to it (issue #22).
ARM, POWER and other non-x86 targets. There is no NEON kernel, so every call uses the portable Rust code (MAX_DEGREE = 1), which issue #7 found slightly slower than blake2-rfc on a Neoverse N1.

x86 CPUs without AVX2 hashing a single message. Single-message BLAKE2b has only an AVX2 kernel (a code comment says the SSE compress1 was never ported), so SSE4.1-only machines fall back to portable code for plain BLAKE2b. SSE4.1 is only used for 2-way many/BLAKE2bp and for BLAKE2s.
C/C++ projects. There is no C header or FFI layer, so Neves' blake2-avx2 C code (the ancestor, vendored in benches/) or libsodium is the natural pick there.

integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2024. CI's MSRV job builds with 1.85.1, but Cargo.toml declares no rust-version and the author does not treat MSRV bumps as breaking (issue #30).
integration.platforms: x86/x86-64 with runtime AVX2 and SSE4.1 dispatch; all other targets use portable Rust (tested in CI on aarch64 macOS, armv7, aarch64 Linux, i586/i686, powerpc64 and s390x); no_std is supported
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Params, State and Hash are plain owned structs with no shared mutable state (only CPU-feature detection through std), so use one State per thread.

gotchas: With default-features = false (no_std), runtime detection is off and only portable code runs, unless the build enables the CPU features at compile time, for example RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+avx2" (per a guts.rs comment).
Params setters panic on out-of-range values (hash_length over 64, key over 64 bytes, and so on). Hash equality is constant-time, but as_bytes()/as_array() comparisons are not.
Debug builds are dramatically slower. In issue #22 a user measured 17 s in a debug build versus 158 ms with --release on an ~80 MB file.

BLAKE2bp throughput changes by several percent with the input buffer's offset modulo 512 bytes (issue #8), which is why the benchmark averages over all 512 offsets. Your allocator's alignment decides where you land.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over BLAKE3 only when the BLAKE2 digest itself is required; BLAKE3 is about 3x faster on the same machine and has more SIMD backends. Over the SHA-256 siblings (sha2-with-c-intrinsic, ISA-L multi-buffer SHA, sha256-simd), pick it when you can drop SHA-2 compatibility and want a maintained, widely used Rust crate with built-in multi-message batching.
verified_claims_summary: The README's bench_multiprocess table comes from one Intel Core i5-8250U laptop, which has no SHA-NI: rustc 1.40.0 with cargo --release, OpenSSL 1.1.1d, libsodium 1.0.18, hashing 1 MB in-memory inputs in 100 processes across all 512 offsets. It shows BLAKE2b at 2.81 cpb against OpenSSL SHA-512 at 5.11 (1.82x), many::hash/BLAKE2bp at 1.43/1.44 cpb (about 3.5x vs SHA-512, 2.45x vs SHA-1 at 3.51), and only 1.09x over libsodium's BLAKE2b at 3.07. The harness itself prints GB/s, and the README does not say how it converted that to cycles per byte.
status_note: Actively maintained, if slowly: v1.0.5 (2026-08-20) removed arrayref after its newest crates.io release turned out to be malicious, and there were dependency and edition updates in 2025-26. It is MIT, copyable, and has ~58M (blake2b_simd) and ~23M (blake2s_simd) downloads. The 2020 benchmark was never rerun, and the bench crate was bumped to edition 2024 without code changes; it still calls env::set_var outside an unsafe block, which that edition rejects, so it may not build unmodified (not verified by building).
